## What "writing a trigger" means

A worker uses triggers two ways. Most of the time, you bind the worker's functions by registering a
trigger on an existing trigger type such as: [`http`](https://workers.iii.dev/workers/http),
[`cron`](https://workers.iii.dev/workers/cron),
[queue messages](https://workers.iii.dev/workers/queue),
[`state` changes](https://workers.iii.dev/workers/state), and any other event source in the system.
Less often, you register a new trigger type from your worker so other workers can bind their
functions to events your worker emits.

This page shows how to make your own trigger types. To bind functions to existing trigger types, see
[Using iii / Triggers](../using-iii/triggers).

<Note>
  For direct calls (`worker.trigger`, `iii trigger`) and `TriggerAction`, see [Using iii /
  Functions](../using-iii/functions#triggering-invoking-functions). For conditions and multiple
  bindings per function, see [Using iii / Triggers](../using-iii/triggers).
</Note>

{/* TODO: Re-review against the SDK surface after the SDK rework */}

## Bind a function to an existing trigger type

Most workers bind their functions to trigger types that other workers publish. Call
`worker.registerTrigger({ type, function_id, config })`. You can bind before the publishing worker
connects. The engine stores the binding and activates it when the trigger type registers. For the
per-SDK code, multiple bindings, conditions, and the unregister handle, see
[Using iii / Triggers](../using-iii/triggers#register-a-trigger).

## Attach metadata to a trigger

A consumer can add an optional `metadata` object to each binding. See
[Trigger metadata](../using-iii/triggers#trigger-metadata). Your `registerTrigger(config)` callback
gets it as `config.metadata`. Store it with the binding. Send it with `worker.trigger` when the
trigger fires, so the bound function gets it. The engine does not add it to the call.
[`engine::registered-triggers::info`](../reference/engine-protocol#engine-discovery-functions) also
returns it.

<Note>
  Metadata belongs to one binding, and the consumer sets it. Trigger type
  [schemas](#attach-schemas-to-the-trigger-type) (`trigger_request_format` and
  `call_request_format`) belong to the trigger type, and the publisher sets them. The schemas
  describe the `config` that consumers send and the payload that bound functions get.
</Note>

## Declaring a Trigger Type

A _publisher_ worker declares a trigger type. Functions that other workers register then fire on
events the publisher observes (an HTTP request, a webhook hit, a file change, a database update).
For how trigger types fit into iii, see [Trigger types](../understanding-iii#trigger-types).

### Register the trigger type

Call `worker.registerTriggerType({ id, description }, handler)` once at startup. Consumers use the
`id` as the `type` when they bind a function (for example, `type: "mini-http"`).

{/* TODO: Re-review against the SDK surface after the SDK rework */}

The `handler` implements the `TriggerHandler` interface. It has two callbacks. The engine calls them
on your publisher worker when a consumer binds or unbinds:

- `registerTrigger(config)`: Runs when any consumer worker binds a function to your trigger type.
  The `config` carries the trigger instance `id`, the consumer `function_id`, the consumer `config`,
  the optional `metadata`, and the `namespace` of the target function. The `namespace` is absent
  when the target function is in the `default` namespace. Store all of it in a bindings table in
  your worker.
- `unregisterTrigger(config)`: Runs on unbind. Remove the binding from your table.

To see the bindings that the engine records, call
[`engine::registered-triggers::list`](../reference/engine-protocol#engine-discovery-functions). Pass
`include_pending: true` to also see the stored bindings that are `pending`.

The engine removes the trigger type when your worker disconnects. See
[Unregister a Trigger Type](#unregister-a-trigger-type).

### Example: A mini `http` from scratch

{/* TODO: Re-review against the SDK surface after the SDK rework */}

The example below sketches a tiny version of [http](https://workers.iii.dev/workers/http), the
worker that publishes the real `http` trigger type. The publisher worker:

1. Declares an HTTP-shaped trigger type called `mini-http`
1. Maintains a `bindings` map of `{ trigger id → function_id, method+path }` as consumers
   bind/unbind
1. Is then ready to look up the right binding when an HTTP request is received. Firing the bound
   function is covered in [Dispatch events to bound functions](#dispatch-events-to-bound-functions)
   below.

<Accordion title="Example: declare a `mini-http` trigger type">
  <Tabs>
    <Tab title="Node / TypeScript">
      ```typescript
      import { registerWorker } from "iii-sdk";
      import type { TriggerConfig, TriggerHandler } from "iii-sdk/trigger";

      const url = process.env.III_URL;
      if (!url) throw new Error("III_URL must be set");
      const worker = registerWorker(url, { namespace: "orders" });

      type MiniHttpConfig = {
        api_path: string; // leading slash, e.g. "/orders"
        http_method?: "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "DELETE";
      };

      const bindings = new Map<string, TriggerConfig<MiniHttpConfig>>();

      const httpHandler: TriggerHandler<MiniHttpConfig> = {
        async registerTrigger(config) {
          bindings.set(config.id, config);
        },
        async unregisterTrigger(config) {
          bindings.delete(config.id);
        },
      };

      worker.registerTriggerType(
        { id: "mini-http", description: "Routes HTTP requests to bound functions" },
        httpHandler,
      );
      ```
    </Tab>
    <Tab title="Python">
      ```python
      import os
      from iii import InitOptions, register_worker
      from iii.protocol import RegisterTriggerTypeInput
      from iii.trigger import TriggerConfig, TriggerHandler

      worker = register_worker(
          os.environ.get("III_URL"),
          InitOptions(
              worker_name="mini-http-worker",
              namespace="orders",
          ),
      )

      bindings: dict[str, TriggerConfig] = {}

      class HttpHandler(TriggerHandler):
          async def register_trigger(self, config: TriggerConfig) -> None:
              bindings[config.id] = config

          async def unregister_trigger(self, config: TriggerConfig) -> None:
              bindings.pop(config.id, None)

      worker.register_trigger_type(
          RegisterTriggerTypeInput(
              id="mini-http",
              description="Routes HTTP requests to bound functions",
          ),
          HttpHandler(),
      )
      ```
    </Tab>
    <Tab title="Rust">
      ```rust
      use std::collections::HashMap;
      use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
      use iii_sdk::errors::Error;
      use iii_sdk::trigger::{TriggerConfig, TriggerHandler};
      use iii_sdk::{InitOptions, RegisterTriggerType, register_worker};

      let url = std::env::var("III_URL").expect("III_URL must be set");
      let worker = register_worker(
          &url,
          InitOptions {
              namespace: Some("orders".into()),
              ..Default::default()
          },
      );

      struct HttpHandler {
          bindings: Arc<Mutex<HashMap<String, TriggerConfig>>>,
      }

      #[async_trait::async_trait]
      impl TriggerHandler for HttpHandler {
          async fn register_trigger(&self, config: TriggerConfig) -> Result<(), Error> {
              self.bindings.lock().unwrap().insert(config.id.clone(), config);
              Ok(())
          }

          async fn unregister_trigger(&self, config: TriggerConfig) -> Result<(), Error> {
              self.bindings.lock().unwrap().remove(&config.id);
              Ok(())
          }
      }

      let bindings: Arc<Mutex<HashMap<String, TriggerConfig>>> = Arc::default();

      worker.register_trigger_type(RegisterTriggerType::new(
          "mini-http",
          "Routes HTTP requests to bound functions",
          HttpHandler { bindings: bindings.clone() },
      ));
      ```
    </Tab>

  </Tabs>
</Accordion>

### Attach schemas to the trigger type

A trigger type can carry two optional JSON Schemas that describe its payloads:

- **`trigger_request_format`**: The schema for the per-binding `config` consumers pass to
  `worker.registerTrigger(...)` when they bind a function to your trigger type.
- **`call_request_format`**: The schema for the payload your worker delivers to bound functions when
  the trigger fires.

Both appear in the iii console, in the agent skills, and in the
[`engine::triggers::info`](../reference/engine-protocol#engine-discovery-functions) output, so
consumers know what to send and what they get.

<Note>
  Runtime validation is not yet supported. Attached schemas are informational only; the engine does
  not reject `config` values or call payloads that don't match them. Treat the schemas as contract
  documentation for consumers, agents, and the console; same caveat as [function request / response
  schemas](./functions#attach-request-and-response-schemas).
</Note>

Each SDK accepts these in its own idiomatic way:

| SDK                                                                                                         | What you pass                                                                                                                                  |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Node](../reference/sdk-node#registertriggertype) / [Browser](../reference/sdk-browser#registertriggertype) | Raw JSON Schema objects on `trigger_request_format` / `call_request_format`. Convert Zod 4+ schemas with `z.toJSONSchema(...)`.                |
| [Python](../reference/sdk-python#register_trigger_type)                                                     | A Pydantic model class (auto-converted) or a raw dict on the same fields of `RegisterTriggerTypeInput`.                                        |
| [Rust](../reference/sdk-rust#register_trigger_type)                                                         | Builder methods on `RegisterTriggerType`: `.trigger_request_format::<T>()` and `.call_request_format::<T>()`, where `T: schemars::JsonSchema`. |

{/* TODO: Re-review against the SDK surface after the SDK rework */}

### Unregister a Trigger Type

The engine removes a trigger type when the worker that registered it disconnects. The engine stores
the bindings to that type. When a worker registers the type again, the engine activates them again.

The SDKs have `worker.unregisterTriggerType(...)` (Node) and `worker.unregister_trigger_type(...)`
(Python, Rust). At this release, the engine ignores the message that these calls send. The type
stays registered in the engine until the worker disconnects. The call removes the handler from your
worker only. To remove a trigger type at runtime, stop the worker with `worker.shutdown()`.

## Dispatch events to bound functions

There is no special "fire" API. When the underlying event source delivers something (an incoming
HTTP request, a cron tick, a webhook hit), your publisher worker looks up the relevant entry in the
`bindings` table it built inside its `registerTrigger` callback and invokes each matching function
via `worker.trigger(...)`.

Continuing the `mini-http` example from above:

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="Node / TypeScript">
    ```typescript
    // Inside the worker's HTTP listener, after matching method+path to an
    // entry in the `bindings` map from the declare-trigger-type example:
    const binding = bindings.get(matchedTriggerId);
    if (binding) {
      await worker.trigger({
        function_id: binding.function_id,
        payload: { method, headers, body },
        namespace: binding.namespace ?? "default",
        metadata: binding.metadata,
      });
    }
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Python">
    ```python
    # Inside the worker's HTTP listener, after matching method+path to an
    # entry in the `bindings` dict from the declare-trigger-type example:
    binding = bindings[matched_trigger_id]
    worker.trigger({
        "function_id": binding.function_id,
        "payload": {"method": method, "headers": headers, "body": body},
        "namespace": binding.namespace or "default",
        "metadata": binding.metadata,
    })
    ```
  </Tab>
  <Tab title="Rust">
    ```rust
    use iii_sdk::protocol::TriggerRequest;
    use serde_json::json;

    // Inside the worker's HTTP listener, after matching method+path to an
    // entry in the `bindings` map from the declare-trigger-type example:
    let binding = bindings.lock().unwrap().get(&matched_trigger_id).cloned();
    if let Some(binding) = binding {
        let namespace = binding.namespace.clone().unwrap_or_else(|| "default".to_string());
        let mut request = TriggerRequest {
            function_id: binding.function_id.clone(),
            payload: json!({ "method": method, "headers": headers, "body": body }),
            action: None,
            timeout_ms: None,
        }
        .namespace(namespace);
        if let Some(metadata) = binding.metadata.clone() {
            request = request.metadata(metadata);
        }
        worker.trigger(request).await?;
    }
    ```

  </Tab>
</Tabs>

The engine routes each `worker.trigger` call to the bound function and returns the result to your
worker. The engine does not read the binding `config` or `condition_function_id`. Your worker must
match each event against the binding `config`. If your trigger type supports
`condition_function_id`, your worker must call that function first. Skip the bound function when the
condition returns `false`.
